# Token Lifecycle

Source: https://fulla.dev/docs/domains/token-lifecycle

# Token Lifecycle

How tokens are born, live, and die in fulla: the three token types, what is
actually stored, how refresh rotation detects theft, and every knob that
controls a lifetime. For the storage schema behind this, see
[Data Persistence](../architecture/data-persistence.md); for the HTTP
contract, see the [API Reference](api-reference.md) and
[ADR-0004](../adr/ADR-0004.md).

## 1. Three token types, three different shapes

| Token | Shape | Validated by | Lifetime default |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access token | **Opaque random string** (`generateSecureToken`) | Server-side state (introspection / userinfo) — never a self-contained JWT | 3600 s (`access_token_ttl`) |
| Refresh token | Opaque random string + **family id** | Server-side state; rotation on every use | 30 days (configurable) |
| id_token | **RS256 JWT** signed via JWKS (`kid` published at `/.well-known/jwks.json`) | Client-side signature verification (standard OIDC) | Same as access token; issued only with the `openid` scope |

Design rationale ([ADR-0004](../adr/ADR-0004.md)): opaque access tokens keep
the server in full control — revocation is immediate and stateful, and no
key-compromised token outlives its server-side record. The JWT capability is
reserved for the OIDC `id_token`, where the protocol requires it.

One frequent confusion: the **roles** that accompany a token response are part
of the JSON envelope (`"roles": [...]`) and the id_token claims — the opaque
access token itself carries nothing that needs decoding.

## 2. Issuance paths

All grants converge on `TokenService` (libs/oauth2):

| Grant | Mints | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `authorization_code` (+ PKCE, mandatory for PUBLIC clients) | access + refresh (+ id_token if `openid`) | The code is single-use with atomic consume (see §5) |
| `refresh_token` | new access + **new** refresh | Old refresh is revoked; family id is inherited (§4) |
| `client_credentials` | access only (M2M, no user) | CONFIDENTIAL clients only; for organization-owned applications the token additionally carries the `org_id` claim (v1.4.0), exposed via introspection — the subject stays the client id |
| `device_code` | access + refresh after user approval | Polling per RFC 8628 |

`expires_in` in every response advertises the **configured** access-token
lifetime — not a hardcoded 3600 (RFC 6749 §5.1).

## 3. What is stored (and what is not)

- Access and refresh tokens are persisted **only as SHA-256 hashes**
  (`hashToken()` before any repository write) — a database dump exposes no
  usable credentials ([ADR-0004](../adr/ADR-0004.md)).
- The refresh token row additionally stores its `token_family` id, the
  associated access-token hash, `revoked`/`revoked_at`/`revoked_by`.
- Rows past their TTL are deleted by `OAuth2CleanupService`
  (`cleanup_interval_seconds`, default 3600 s) — Postgres via periodic DELETE,
  Redis historically via TTL, memory via periodic sweep.

## 4. Refresh rotation, reuse detection, family revocation

Every refresh grants a **new** refresh token that inherits the same
`token_family` (V008). If a refresh token that was already revoked is
presented again, that is treated as theft: the server **cascades revocation
to every token in the family** — attacker and legitimate user alike must
re-authenticate. The full threat-model walkthrough (with a sequence diagram)
lives in [Security Architecture §7](../architecture/security-architecture.md).

## 5. Single-use of authorization codes

`consumeAuthCode` is atomic per backend: Postgres uses
`UPDATE ... WHERE consumed = false ... RETURNING`, Redis used a Lua script,
memory uses a mutex — so a stolen code replayed in a race loses, always. The
contract is enforced across all three implementations by
`GrantRepositoryContractTest` (`ctest -L Contract`).

## 6. Revocation surfaces

| Surface | Granularity |
|---|---|
| `POST /oauth2/revoke` (RFC 7009) | The presented token |
| Admin API `DELETE /api/admin/tokens/{prefix}` | By token prefix |
| Admin token management | Revoke by **client** or by **user** — wipes every token minted for that principal |

Revocation is stateful and immediate: the very next introspection or
userinfo call with a revoked token returns `{"active": false}` / 401.

## 7. Cache interplay

With the Redis L2 cache enabled (`cache.enabled`), token and client reads hit
`fulla:cache:*` before Postgres. Every write path (issue, refresh, revoke)
invalidates through **delayed double-delete** (immediate DEL + a second DEL
~200 ms later, `cache.invalidation_double_delete_delay_ms`), closing the
race where a concurrent reader re-fills a stale entry between the write and
the first delete. Failures of the second delete are counted in
`fulla_cache_invalidation_failures_total` — see
[Observability](../operate/observability.md). Details in
[Data Persistence · cache consistency](../architecture/data-persistence.md).

## 8. Configuration reference

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `access_token_ttl` | 3600 | Access-token lifetime (seconds); advertised in `expires_in` |
| refresh-token TTL | 30 days | Refresh-token lifetime |
| `cleanup_interval_seconds` | 3600 | How often `OAuth2CleanupService` purges expired rows |
| `cache.enabled` / `cache.ttl_seconds` | false / — | L2 cache for token/client reads ([Configuration Guide](../operate/configuration-guide.md)) |


---

# Refresh Tokens and Revocation Boundaries

Source: https://fulla.dev/docs/domains/token-refresh-and-revocation

# Refresh Tokens and Revocation Boundaries

The S03 security hardening keeps single-use refresh tokens and family reuse detection. It changes how rotation is persisted and makes cache convergence explicit. This page describes the unreleased behavior and the migration required for custom C++ repositories.

## 1. Rotation and Failure Outcomes

The token endpoint authenticates the client before refreshing. The repository then checks that the RT belongs to that client, is unexpired and is unused. A wrong client cannot consume an unused RT or revoke another client's family by presenting a used RT.

Subject normalization, claim resolution and random token generation happen before consumption. Memory rotation holds one mutex; PostgreSQL rotation holds a transaction-scoped family advisory lock, consumes the old RT and inserts both new tokens in one transaction. Success is reported only after a confirmed commit. Rotation and family revocation use the same lock domain.

| Failure or event | Persisted state | Client outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Lookup/storage error before consumption | Old RT unchanged; no new pair | `server_error`; no tokens |
| Random generation or subject normalization failure | Old RT unchanged; no new pair | Error; no tokens |
| Client mismatch or an unused RT with `now >= expires_at` | No consumption or family revocation | `invalid_grant` |
| Access insert, refresh insert, or confirmed commit rejection | Old consumption rolls back; no new pair | `server_error`; no tokens |
| COMMIT confirmation lost | Complete old state or complete rotated state; outcome unknown to caller | `server_error`; no unconfirmed tokens |
| Commit succeeds but HTTP response is lost | Old RT used; complete new pair exists | Reauthentication may be required |
| Correct client's retained used RT is replayed | Entire family, including committed rotated pairs, is revoked | `invalid_grant`; revocation storage failure is `server_error` |

An unknown commit outcome is different from a definite rollback. Never infer that an RT is reusable from a network error. Retrying a used RT can revoke the family, including the pair whose response was lost. There is no grace period or server-side retry idempotency. Coalescing refreshes within one client instance does not coordinate other tabs or processes.

Two requests using one old RT can produce at most one successful rotation. A successful response does not promise that its pair remains active if another request subsequently detects reuse. Expiry alone is not proof of reuse. A retained used record remains reuse evidence even after expiry, preserving the existing Postgres policy; it can never be exchanged again.

Cleanup retains expired RT metadata while its associated AT remains active, including configurations whose RT lifetime is shorter than the AT lifetime. This preserves family revocation reachability without extending RT validity. After that AT expires, is revoked or disappears, a later sweep can reclaim the metadata. No permanent tombstone or schema change is introduced.

## 2. C++ Repository Migration

Custom `ITokenRepository` implementations must implement these additive methods:

- `inspectRefreshToken`: authoritative lookup with `Ready`, `NotFound`, `AlreadyUsed`, `ClientMismatch`, `Expired` and `StorageError`; only a correctly bound client receives used-token metadata.
- `rotateRefreshToken`: revalidate the authoritative old record and expiry inside the critical section, atomically consume and save the pair, and return `Rotated` only after confirmed persistence.
- `revokeTokenFamilyChecked`: atomically revoke both token kinds under the rotation family lock and report confirmed success/failure.

The original CRUD/CAS methods remain available. The new methods have fail-closed defaults, so an old implementation still compiles, but its refresh requests return `server_error` until migrated. This is source compatibility, not behavioral compatibility. There is no binary ABI guarantee. Do not implement the new result by treating every old `nullopt` as reuse, or by claiming atomicity for sequential writes.

Drogon hosts must use `lookupOwnerStatusChecked` for introspection ownership decisions. `OwnerStatusResult` separates Active, confirmed Unmanaged, Suspended (including unknown row statuses) and Unavailable. Only the first two permit introspection. Deployments without an owner registry (`storage_type` other than postgres) classify as Unmanaged — a structural fact known at startup, consistent with memory mode; Unavailable is reserved for registry query errors and timeouts, so a mode without a registry never reports valid tokens as inactive. The old optional `lookupOwnerStatus` wrapper is retained for display/source compatibility and loses the error/absence distinction; it must not authorize access.

The supplied Memory/Postgres repositories and Redis cache decorator implement the new path. The deprecated standalone Redis storage still rejects the refresh grant. Publish this security behavior change in the next MINOR release with the migration notice, following the [versioning policy](../contribute/versioning-and-release.md).

## 3. Token Cache Convergence

PostgreSQL access-token validation and introspection read the master, including cache fallback. A lagging reader is not an authoritative source for security cache refill. This increases master read traffic on misses and failures; size the primary accordingly.

The token L2 cache uses the configured `cache.ttl_seconds.access_token_max` (default 60 seconds), capped by token expiry. The expiration budget starts before the asynchronous lookup. Redis `EXAT` retains that absolute deadline even if a database callback or Redis command arrives late. A Lua operation checks the revocation marker and deadline atomically with refill; introspection also verifies the access-key discriminator, so RT introspection is never cached. Access/introspection payloads preserve `org_id`; older unversioned payloads are treated as misses.

Direct access-token revocation attempts a negative marker and immediate/delayed deletion. Family revocation bypasses positive-cache invalidation and converges through the existing TTL policy. If invalidation fails, an already cached pre-revocation token can remain usable until the earlier of its absolute cache deadline and token expiry. Under synchronized application/Redis clocks and authoritative master reads, a pre-revocation snapshot cannot extend that deadline beyond one configured cache budget after revocation. Account for clock skew operationally; a TTL is not a promise that every replica rejects the next request.

Cached read requests have one five-second local completion deadline spanning Redis lookup, the backing read and guarded refill. Initial Redis errors fall back to the authoritative repository. A guarded-refill error or local deadline rejects the read; it does not return an unconfirmed stale snapshot. Late callbacks cannot complete twice, and the business callback is released. Hosts must run the Drogon event loop used for these timers. Timeout/error counters use `fulla_cache_total{repo="token",outcome="error"}`; failed DEL attempts retain `fulla_cache_invalidation_failures_total{kind="token"}`. A failed negative-marker SET is observable too.

## 4. Permission Changes Are Separate Operations

Token validity, login eligibility and current authorization are distinct checks. Existing policies are not changed into universal immediate revocation:

| Change | API and refresh behavior | Userinfo/introspection and cache boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Disable a user | Sets the login lock; it does not automatically revoke all issued ATs/RTs | Do not treat profile-cache invalidation as token revocation. Explicitly revoke affected tokens when terminating existing access |
| Revoke a user's role | Role-protected APIs resolve current role/permission data; existing token scopes are not rewritten | User-role cache defaults to 120 seconds; write hooks invalidate known subject forms. Userinfo claims are not a replacement for an API authorization check |
| Remove organization membership | Organization-aware gates and claim resolution check membership; the stored `org_id` remains a historical token binding | New userinfo/refresh ID-token `org_ctx` is omitted when membership is absent. Introspection `org_id` does not prove current membership |
| Suspend an open-platform client | New client lookup rejects a positively suspended owner; an existing AT is not universally revoked by that lookup | Introspection has a typed owner-status overlay: query errors/timeouts produce only `active:false`, never an active result. Client and owner-status caches remain separate; other APIs do not acquire this overlay |

Owner-status memoization has a 60-second read-start budget and a five-second completion deadline. Only successful Found/NoRow results are cached; errors/timeouts and their late callbacks cannot refill the memo. Invalidation can still race an in-flight successful read within its original budget. Other existing caches retain their own policies: client L2 defaults to 300 seconds, user roles to 120 seconds and user profiles to 300 seconds. These are entry lifetimes, not proven commit-to-rejection deadlines: their asynchronous refill and backing read duration must also be considered. The token-cache absolute-budget guarantee above must not be generalized to these caches. A backing read or replica without a bounded freshness/latency guarantee cannot establish a stricter global revocation SLO merely by configuring a TTL.

The role-removal row refers to removing a user's role assignment. Editing the permissions granted by an existing role uses a separate process-local `RolePermissionResolver` cache with no TTL. Its current policy requires invalidation on every replica (or restart); the user-role TTL does not bound permission-definition changes. This work does not add a cross-process invalidation protocol.

If immediate session termination is required, perform and verify explicit token revocation. Without that operation, disabling login or changing roles must not be advertised as revoking existing tokens. A request already being authorized when a change commits is also different from a new request starting afterwards.

## 5. Validation and Operational Limits

The regression suite covers Memory/Postgres binding, collisions at either pair insert, deferred commit rejection, single-use concurrency, family-lock expiry and a controlled CAS-to-INSERT pause during family revocation. Domain tests cover lookup/rotation errors, random-source failure, unknown commit outcomes, response-loss/replay semantics and old-only SDK implementations. Owner-status tests separately cover policy mapping, missing backends and real PostgreSQL lock timeouts without confusing a preceding client-authentication error with overlay behavior. Cache tests use independent node objects sharing real Redis, plus command faults and deferred snapshots; this models shared L2 behavior and does not claim a multi-host deployment test.

Keep failure records distinct: deterministic database rejection, unknown database commit outcome and lost HTTP response have different evidence. Do not claim a simulated acknowledgement-loss test is a real network-partition experiment. No token format, default token lifetime, consent policy, organization permission rule or production deployment is changed by this work.


---

# SDK Integration Guide (Consuming Release Artifacts)

Source: https://fulla.dev/docs/sdk/sdk-integration-guide

# SDK Integration Guide (Consuming Release Artifacts)

How to obtain and integrate fulla's release artifacts: the SDK binary package (libraries + headers + `fulla-*Config.cmake`) and the GHCR container images. For runtime behavior guarantees (threading / ABI / exceptions / logging / plugin registration), see the [SDK Runtime Contract](sdk-runtime-contract.md) — this document covers only how to obtain and wire everything up. The release pipeline is `.github/workflows/release.yml` (triggered by a strict SemVer tag `vX.Y.Z`).

> Non-C++ consumers: the officially maintained **Python** (PyPI [`fulla-oauth2`](https://pypi.org/project/fulla-oauth2/)), **Go** (`github.com/voidvec/fulla/clients/go`) and **TypeScript/JavaScript** (npm [`fulla-oauth2`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/fulla-oauth2), v1.6.0+) HTTP clients work out of the box; see [clients/](https://github.com/voidvec/fulla/tree/master/clients). For a runnable browser-app integration see [`examples/nextjs-demo`](https://github.com/voidvec/fulla/tree/master/examples/nextjs-demo) (login → callback → session → protected API → logout in ≤30 minutes).

---

## 1. Release Artifact Inventory

| Artifact | Location | Notes |
|------|------|------|
| SDK package `fulla-sdk-<ver>-linux-x86_64.tar.gz` | GitHub Release attachment | 8 static libraries + `include/fulla/**` headers + `lib/cmake/fulla-*/{Config,ConfigVersion,Targets}.cmake` (with `.sha256`) |
| Backend image | `ghcr.io/voidvec/fulla-backend:<ver>` | Multi-arch (amd64 + arm64), entry port `:5555`, `/health` liveness probe |
| User frontend image | `ghcr.io/voidvec/fulla-frontend:<ver>` | nginx static hosting, `:80` |
| Admin console image | `ghcr.io/voidvec/fulla-admin:<ver>` | nginx static hosting of `/admin`, `:80` |

The images also carry a `latest` tag; `<ver>-amd64` / `<ver>-arm64` are single-arch intermediate tags. The server executable is **not** part of the SDK package — product deployment goes through the image channel.

## 2. SDK Package Prerequisites (Read This First)

- **v1.x guarantees only source-level SemVer, not binary ABI** (Contract §2). The published `linux-x86_64` static libraries are compiled with the Release pipeline's toolchain (ubuntu-24.04 / gcc / libstdc++ / C++17 / Conan-locked dependencies); if your toolchain does not match, **fall back to source integration** (`add_subdirectory`, or run `cmake --install` yourself — the same SDK surface).
- Third-party dependencies (Drogon / OpenSSL / jsoncpp, etc.) are **not** included in the package. Consumers resolve the same dependency versions using the repository root's `conanfile.py` + `conan.lock`, ensuring the `find_dependency` closure matches what the libraries were compiled against.

## 3. find_package Integration Steps

```bash
# 1) 解包
tar xzf fulla-sdk-1.6.0-linux-x86_64.tar.gz   # -> fulla-sdk-1.6.0-linux-x86_64/

# 2) 用仓库的 conanfile.py 解析依赖（生成 toolchain + 各依赖的 CMake config）
conan install <fulla-repo> --output-folder=deps --build=missing \
  -s build_type=Release -s compiler.cppstd=17

# 3) 配置消费工程：toolchain 供依赖解析，PREFIX_PATH 指向解包目录
cmake -S . -B build \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=$PWD/deps/conan_toolchain.cmake \
  -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=$PWD/fulla-sdk-1.6.0-linux-x86_64
cmake --build build -j
```

On the CMakeLists side:

```cmake
# 全栈宿主：一个包拉全闭包（common/oauth2/identity/storage-*/Drogon/OpenSSL/CURL）
find_package(fulla-drogon CONFIG REQUIRED)
target_link_libraries(my-host PRIVATE fulla::drogon)

# 或只取引擎面（无 Drogon 依赖）：
find_package(fulla-oauth2 CONFIG REQUIRED)
find_package(fulla-storage-memory CONFIG REQUIRED)
target_link_libraries(my-engine PRIVATE fulla::oauth2 fulla::storage::memory)
```

Available packages and exported targets: `fulla-common`→`fulla::common` (also provides `fulla::common::testing`), `fulla-oauth2`→`fulla::oauth2`, `fulla-identity`→`fulla::identity`, `fulla-storage-{memory,redis,postgres}`→`fulla::storage::{memory,redis,postgres}`, and `fulla-drogon`→`fulla::drogon`. Version compatibility is SameMajorVersion (`find_package(fulla-drogon 1.0 CONFIG REQUIRED)` pins the major version).

Reference consumers (continuously verified by the repository CI):

- `examples/full-stack-host/`: a complete HTTP host that uses `find_package(fulla-drogon)` to reuse the product controllers / OAuth2Plugin / views. The Release pipeline uses it to run a consumption smoke test against the **install prefix** (`ctest -L SdkSmoke` performs the same verification against the build tree).
- `examples/third-party-host/`: a minimal engine consumer that links only the four Domain-layer packages.

## 4. Plugin Registration and whole-archive (H1/F1/H5 Framing)

`fulla::drogon` is a STATIC library containing the plugin, controllers and
adapters. The old separate OBJECT target is no longer the linking model.

Follow `examples/full-stack-host/`: compile the product bootstrap sources,
call `registerAllControllers()`, and wire plugin dependencies at startup.
The config entry `plugins[].name = "OAuth2Plugin"` selects the reflected
class after linking; a string in JSON cannot retain an otherwise unreferenced
static-library object. Wrappers relying only on static self-registration
must force the required objects into the executable, using whole-archive or
the platform's equivalent, and run a registration smoke test.

See [SDK Runtime Contract](sdk-runtime-contract.md#6-plugin-registration-and-configuration-contract-host-integration)
for configuration compatibility guarantees.

## 5. Using the Images

```bash
docker pull ghcr.io/voidvec/fulla-backend:1.6.0
```

The three images correspond one-to-one to the build targets in `deploy/docker/docker-compose.yml` (`backend-runtime` / `frontend-runtime` / `frontends/admin/Dockerfile`); environment variables and mount conventions are taken directly from the compose file's `fulla-backend` service section (`FULLA_DB_HOST` / `FULLA_REDIS_HOST` / `FULLA_AUTO_MIGRATE`, etc.).

## 6. Release Process (Maintainers)

1. Confirm that the three version sources agree (`cmake/Version.cmake` is the single source of truth; api-diff enforces in CI that it matches the root `CMakeLists.txt` and `conanfile.py`) and that the API baseline has been updated according to SemVer rules (`tools/api-diff/`).
2. (Optional) Refresh CHANGELOG.md locally:
   `git cliff --unreleased --tag vX.Y.Z --prepend CHANGELOG.md`
   (configuration lives in the root `cliff.toml`; the release workflow only generates the Release notes and never back-fills commits from the tag ref).
3. Create a strict SemVer tag: `git tag vX.Y.Z && git push origin vX.Y.Z`. Tags with a suffix (e.g. `v1.0.0-rc1`) do **not** trigger a release.
4. `release.yml` then runs automatically: tag/version consistency checks → SDK packaging + install-tree consumption smoke test → native builds of the three images for amd64/arm64 → multi-arch manifest (`<ver>` + `latest`) → cosign keyless signing of the three images by digest + syft-generated SPDX SBOMs (three images + source tree) → GitHub Release (notes generated by git-cliff, with the SDK attachment and all SBOMs attached).
5. A manual `workflow_dispatch` trigger = dry run (full build, but nothing is pushed and no Release is published).

### Verifying Release Artifacts (Consumers)

```sh
# 镜像签名（keyless：身份 = release.yml 工作流，无需公钥分发）
cosign verify ghcr.io/voidvec/fulla-backend:<ver> \
  --certificate-identity-regexp \
    'https://github.com/voidvec/[^/]+/.github/workflows/release.yml.*' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com

# SDK tarball 校验和（Release 附件）
sha256sum -c fulla-sdk-<ver>-linux-x86_64.tar.gz.sha256
```


## Quickstart: Embedding fulla into Your Own Drogon Host

Use `examples/full-stack-host/` for bootstrap and view compilation (package imports
are described in Section 3). The following fragments show configuration and
filter integration after that host registration is in place:

**1. Activate the plugin in the host's `config.json`** (register product controllers through the host bootstrap before starting Drogon):

```json
{
    "plugins": [
        {
            "name": "OAuth2Plugin",
            "dependencies": [],
            "config": {
                "storage_type": "postgres",
                "postgres": { "db_client_name": "default" },
                "redis": { "client_name": "default" }
            }
        }
    ]
}
```

**2. Protect business APIs with `AuthorizationFilter`** (fully qualified name `fulla::drogon::filters::AuthorizationFilter`):

```cpp
METHOD_LIST_BEGIN
ADD_METHOD_TO(UserApi::getProfile, "/api/me", drogon::Get,
              "fulla::drogon::filters::AuthorizationFilter");
METHOD_LIST_END
```

Note: controllers with `AutoCreation=false` require explicit registration before
Drogon starts, as shown in `examples/full-stack-host/`; linking the static library
alone is insufficient. Do not invoke registration macros manually. PostgreSQL
storage requires running `apps/server/migrations/` first (or setting
`FULLA_AUTO_MIGRATE=true`).

> This section was merged in from the retired plugin-integration.md (docs governance A2).
